answer: At every integration step, a stock-flow model should integrate the offered-work rate over the step into an amount, classify each unit at the declared ingress boundary as completed, rejected or backlog, then assert offered = completed + rejected + backlog after every update, not only at the end of the run. Each state variable carries a stock unit, each flow that unit per unit of time, and every parameter that multiplies a flow is reciprocal or dimensionless. Capacity binds per step: admitting a whole interval of arrivals at once, or serving more backlog than exists, produces negative stock. The V12 model uses a fixed 0.1-second step, asserts non-negativity after each update, and treats a persistent conservation gap as a modelling defect: it reports a conservation flag and aborts instead of writing a partial record. The discrete-event variant adds failed and in_system. Conservation is necessary but not sufficient, because a model can conserve offered work while assigning it to the wrong outcome, so timeout and retry paths are checked separately. Boundaries: the update-order convention (arrival crediting at step start or end, same-step service) is not fixed; an initial backlog generalizes the window identity; retries are attempts, not new logical demand; and V12 parameters are synthetic and uncalibrated, so conservation shows internal consistency, not real workload validity.
